25.text: This lab keeps the same algorithm as pure Python, but swaps scalar arithmetic for arrays. The goal is speed without surrendering understanding of the gradients.

26.text: Same dataset, same task. That makes the comparison with lab 01 about representation and backprop mechanics, not about a different problem.

27.text: We keep the data pipeline close to lab 01 so the reader can focus on the real shift: vectorized forward pass, hand-derived backward pass.

30.text: Here is the big transition from lab 01: NumPy compresses the forward pass into matrix operations, but we still refuse to hide the gradient story behind autograd.

32.text: Use the same reproducible setup as lab 01 so the new complexity comes from arrays and manual gradients, not from a different run.

33.text: NumPy has its own RNG because arrays bring their own initialization path. That separation is the first hint that frameworks often manage randomness differently too.

38.text: Same shared corpus as lab 01. That continuity is what lets the framework progression feel like one unfolding story instead of separate demos.

39.text: Keep the tutorial self-contained here too so the only new burden is understanding the math, not setting up the environment.

42.text: Download URL for the names dataset.

45.text: Same tokenization as lab 01, each line becomes one training document.

50.text: BOS token ID, same convention across all labs.

57.text: Same tiny architecture as lab 01, this lab is about the computation method, not the model size.

59.text: A single transformer layer keeps the model minimal. Real GPTs stack dozens, but one is enough to learn interesting name patterns and demonstrate the full algorithm.

64.text: Helper to create a random NumPy array, replaces lab 01's nested list of Value objects. One line, same effect.

65.text: Standard normal scaled by 0.08, same initialization distribution as lab 01.

69.text: Parameters stored as a flat dict of NumPy arrays. Compare to lab 01's nested lists of Value objects, same data, vastly more efficient storage.

70.text: Token embeddings: each row is one token's learned representation.

71.text: Position embeddings: each row encodes a position in the sequence.

72.text: Output projection: maps embeddings back to vocabulary scores.

74.text: Allocate per-layer attention and MLP weights.

75.text: The query weight matrix. Multiplying the input by this produces the 'what am I looking for?' vectors for attention.

76.text: The key weight matrix. It produces 'what do I contain?' vectors that queries will be matched against to determine relevance.

77.text: The value weight matrix. It produces vectors carrying the actual content that attention will retrieve and blend together.

78.text: Output projection recombines multi-head attention outputs. After each head focuses on different relationships, this matrix merges their perspectives into a unified representation.

83.text: Every parameter gets a matching zero-filled gradient array. In lab 01, gradients lived inside each Value. Here, we manage them ourselves.

85.text: Count total parameters to verify we match lab 01.

92.text: RMSNorm forward, returning both the output and a cache of intermediate values. The backward pass needs those cached values to compute gradients.

94.text: Mean of squares across the embedding dimension. NumPy handles this across entire matrices, not one scalar at a time.

95.text: Reciprocal square root, the scaling factor. Same formula as lab 01's (ms + 1e-5) ** -0.5.

96.text: Scale the input. Broadcasting handles the (T, 1) * (T, D) multiplication automatically.

97.text: Return the output together with the cache, following the key pattern that the forward pass stores everything the backward pass will need.

100.text: RMSNorm backward, given the gradient of the output, compute the gradient of the input. This is the manual derivative you'd get from the chain rule on paper.

101.text: Unpack the cached values from the forward pass.

103.text: The hand-derived RMSNorm gradient. Two terms: direct path through the scale, and indirect path through the normalization. This is what autograd computes automatically.

107.text: Softmax forward, same subtract-max-then-exponentiate trick as lab 01, but vectorized over entire matrices.

109.text: Subtract max for numerical stability, prevents overflow in exp().

111.text: Normalize to get probabilities, so that each row sums to 1.

114.text: Softmax backward. The Jacobian of softmax is dense (every output depends on every input), but this compact formula handles it.

116.text: Sum of element-wise product: this captures the coupling between all softmax outputs.

117.text: Elegant formula: p * (dp - sum(dp * p)). Derived from differentiating the softmax function, doing this by hand is a rite of passage.

120.text: ReLU forward: save a binary mask of which neurons fired. The backward pass just uses this mask as a gate.

121.text: The mask is 1 where the input was positive and 0 elsewhere, which is exactly the ReLU derivative.

122.text: Element-wise multiply: zero out negative inputs.

126.text: ReLU backward: gradients pass through where the neuron was active, get blocked where it was dead. Multiply by the mask, that's it.

128.text: Dead simple: dout * mask. If the neuron fired in the forward pass, its gradient flows; if not, it's zero.

131.text: The forward pass processes an entire sequence at once as a matrix, no more position-by-position loop like lab 01.

136.text: How many tokens we're processing. The model will see all of these at once, unlike lab 01 which processed one position at a time.

137.text: The cache dictionary stores every intermediate result the backward pass will need.

140.text: Gather all token embeddings at once with fancy indexing. In lab 01, this was a lookup in a loop.

142.text: Broadcast addition fuses token and position information, same as lab 01 but for all positions simultaneously.

145.text: Normalize and cache. Every intermediate result stored here will be consumed during backpropagation.

148.text: Snapshot the representation before attention transforms it. The residual connection will add this back, ensuring the layer can only refine, not destroy, what came before.

151.text: Normalize and cache before attention. The cache stores the normalization statistics so the backward pass can compute exact gradients without re-doing the forward math.

154.text: Query projection: (n, D) @ (D, D). One matrix multiply replaces lab 01's nested list-comprehension linear layer.

156.text: Project into value vectors, which carry the actual information that attention will retrieve and blend. Same operation as Q and K, different learned weights.

159.text: Reshape and transpose to split into attention heads. The (n, D) matrix becomes (n_head, n, head_dim), each head gets its own slice.

160.text: Keys get the same multi-head split. Each head's keys will be matched against only that head's queries, so different heads learn different notions of relevance.

161.text: Values get the same multi-head split. Each head independently retrieves content from its own subspace, then the results are concatenated.

164.text: Batch matrix multiply: all heads compute attention scores simultaneously. One operation replaces lab 01's per-head loop.

166.text: Causal mask: upper triangle of ones. Prevents tokens from attending to future positions, the core constraint of autoregressive generation.

167.text: Fill future positions with -1e9 so softmax gives them ~zero probability.

168.text: Softmax over the last dimension, each row becomes a probability distribution over which past tokens to attend to.

171.text: Weighted sum of values using attention probabilities, the actual information retrieval step.

173.text: Reverse the reshape: merge heads back into a single (n, D) matrix.

176.text: Output projection: mix the multi-head outputs.

179.text: Residual connection: add attention output to original input.

181.text: Cache everything the attention backward pass needs, eleven values in total, which is the price of doing backprop by hand.

184.text: Snapshot the representation before the MLP transforms it. The residual connection will add this back, letting gradients flow through an unobstructed shortcut path.

185.text: Normalize before the feed-forward network. Like the pre-attention norm, this keeps activations on a consistent scale so the MLP can learn stable transformations.

188.text: MLP expansion: project to 4x wider hidden layer.

189.text: ReLU activation with its binary mask cached for the backward pass. The mask records which neurons fired, which is all the backward pass needs to route gradients.

190.text: MLP contraction: project back to embedding dimension.

192.text: Add the MLP output back to its input via the residual connection. This is the second skip connection in the block, completing the norm-transform-add pattern.

193.text: Cache all MLP intermediates for backward.

196.text: Final projection to vocabulary logits. The .T is pure bookkeeping, not weight tying: lm_head is stored (V, D) like the embedding table, so it has to be transposed before it can multiply an (n, D) hidden state. Nothing in this repo ties the output head to wte.

197.text: Cache the final hidden states for the backward pass.

201.text: Combines forward pass with loss computation, the complete training forward step.

203.text: Total sequence length before clipping. We need this to determine how many input-target pairs we can form from this document.

204.text: Clip to the maximum context window. Most names are short enough to fit, but this guard prevents index-out-of-bounds on unusually long entries.

206.text: Target tokens (all but first), shifted by one position.

208.text: Feed the tokens through the model to get logits and the cache of intermediates. The cache is what makes manual backprop possible without recomputing the forward pass.

211.text: Convert logits to probabilities for cross-entropy loss.

212.text: Gather the log-probabilities of the correct targets. The 1e-10 prevents log(0).

213.text: Mean negative log-probability, cross-entropy loss. Lower means the model assigns higher probability to the right answers.

215.text: Pack everything into the cache for the backward pass.

219.text: The backward pass: about 80 lines, 44 of them nothing but gradient arithmetic, for a one-layer model. Lab 03 replaces the whole thing with loss.backward(), which is the point of writing it out once.

224.text: Softmax + cross-entropy gradient shortcut: start with the probabilities, subtract 1 from the correct class. This elegant shorthand replaces two separate backward passes.

225.text: Subtract 1 at target positions, the combined softmax-CE gradient.

226.text: Average over the sequence, matches the mean in the loss computation.

229.text: Gradient for lm_head: dlogits.T @ x. Accumulate with += because gradients add up.

230.text: Gradient flowing back into the hidden states.

232.text: Walk backward through layers, reverse order of the forward pass.

234.text: Unpack the four intermediate values the MLP forward pass cached. Each one is needed to compute the exact gradient for the corresponding weight matrix.

236.text: Save residual gradient, it bypasses the MLP and adds directly later.

238.text: Gradient through fc2: the backward of act @ fc2 w.r.t. act.

239.text: Weight gradient for fc2: act.T @ dx. This is the outer product pattern: input.T @ output_grad.

241.text: ReLU backward: zero out gradients for dead neurons.

244.text: Gradient through fc1: same pattern as fc2.

245.text: Weight gradient for fc1: the outer product of the normalized input and the hidden gradient. This tells us how to adjust fc1 to reduce the loss.

248.text: RMSNorm backward, uses the cached normalization statistics.

249.text: Add the residual gradient. The residual connection means gradients take two paths, through the MLP and around it, and they add together.

252.text: Unpack the attention cache, all eleven intermediate values.

254.text: Save the residual gradient for the attention skip connection.

258.text: Weight gradient for the output projection.

261.text: Reshape gradient back into multi-head format.

264.text: Gradient through att_probs @ V_h w.r.t. attention probabilities.

265.text: Gradient flowing back into value vectors. The attention probabilities determine how much each value contributed to the output, so transposing them gives the correct routing.

268.text: Softmax backward on attention weights, uses the formula from softmax_bwd.

270.text: Rebuild the same mask to zero the gradients that flowed to future positions. They were set to -1e9 in the forward pass, so softmax gave them a vanishing weight; whatever gradient comes back through them is rounding noise, not signal.

271.text: Zeroed rather than scaled: those keys had no influence on the output, so they are owed no gradient. Forgetting this line is a classic manual-backprop bug that leaks signal backwards through the causal wall.

272.text: Undo the sqrt(head_dim) scaling from the forward pass.

279.text: Reshape head gradients back to (n, D).

280.text: Key gradients get the same reshape back to full embedding dimension. The per-head gradients are simply concatenated since the heads operate on non-overlapping slices.

281.text: Value gradients reshaped identically. All three QKV gradients flow back through the same reshape-transpose pipeline that split them into heads during the forward pass.

284.text: Sum gradients from all three QKV projections. The same x_normed feeds into Q, K, and V, so its gradient is the sum of all three paths.

290.text: RMSNorm backward for the pre-attention norm.

291.text: Add residual gradient, completing the attention skip connection.

294.text: Initial RMSNorm backward, the very first normalization in the forward pass.

297.text: Embedding gradients: scatter the position-level gradients back to the embedding tables. Unlike weight matrices, embeddings use row indexing, so we accumulate manually.

298.text: Each token ID's embedding row gets the gradient from that position.

299.text: Each position's embedding row gets the same gradient.

306.text: First moment buffers, matching dict structure to parameters.

307.text: Second moment buffers. Named Vb to avoid shadowing Python's v loop variable.

313.text: Collect every step's wall-clock time. The claim that arrays beat scalars is the whole reason this lab exists, so the lab measures it instead of asserting it.

314.text: The main training loop. Each iteration: pick a name, forward pass, manual backward pass, Adam update. One thousand steps through this cycle.

315.text: Start the clock before tokenizing so the number covers the entire step: vectorized forward, hand-written backward, and the Adam update. Timing only the matrix multiplies would flatter NumPy.

316.text: Cycle through the dataset with modular indexing. After seeing all names, we loop back to the beginning for another pass.

318.text: Convert to NumPy array for the forward pass.

321.text: Zero all gradients before each step. In lab 01, this was p.grad = 0 per parameter; here it's per array.

322.text: Fill with zeros, faster than creating new arrays.

325.text: The backward pass, all ~80 hand-written lines of it. Lab 03 shrinks this call site to loss.backward() without changing a single number.

328.text: Linear learning rate decay, same schedule as lab 01.

329.text: Iterate over every parameter array in the model to apply the Adam update. NumPy broadcasting handles entire weight matrices at once.

330.text: First moment update, exponential moving average of gradients.

331.text: Second moment update, exponential moving average of squared gradients.

334.text: Adam parameter update. Same formula as lab 01, but operating on entire arrays at once thanks to NumPy broadcasting.

336.text: Store the elapsed milliseconds. Run lab 01 next to this and the difference is not subtle: there, one scalar-autograd step is slow enough to watch.

338.text: Log every 10 steps (lab 01 logged every step, the NumPy version is fast enough that would be too verbose).

341.text: Average the last ten steps rather than printing one. A single step is short enough that scheduler noise dominates it, and a jumpy number teaches the wrong lesson.

343.text: The headline for this lab, printed from your own run rather than quoted from the author's. Whatever the absolute value, it is the yardstick lab 03 onwards gets compared against.

352.text: Generate 20 entirely new names by sampling from the model's learned distribution. These names never appeared in the training data.

353.text: Start with BOS token in the generated sequence.

356.text: Re-run the forward pass over the entire prefix generated so far. There is no cache of any kind here, so position five recomputes everything position four already did; lab 12 is where a KV cache finally removes that waste.

357.text: Take only the last position's logits and apply temperature scaling.

358.text: Reshape for softmax (expects 2D input) and get probabilities.

359.text: Sample from the distribution using NumPy's RNG.

360.text: When the model outputs the BOS token during generation, it is signaling that this name is complete and we should stop adding characters.

362.text: Extend the sequence with the new token.

364.text: Print the finished name. It was invented from the 1000 documents the model actually saw, one per training step, out of the 32K in the corpus.
